opus-5.5.text:
That's a good question, and it's a bit counterintuitive. People assume most of the time goes to the agents talking: the team meetings, the PI agent coordinating the immunologist, computational biologist and machine learning specialist, the critic agent pushing back. That part is surprisingly cheap and fast. A full meeting with several rounds of discussion might take a few minutes and cost a few dollars in API calls.

Most of the actual compute goes into the computational biology pipeline the agents designed and then ran. For the nanobody project, the agents put together a workflow using ESM to score mutations, AlphaFold-Multimer to predict the structure of each nanobody binding the spike protein, and Rosetta to estimate binding energies. Each round they generated many candidate mutations and evaluated them all. The structure prediction and the Rosetta calculations are by far the heaviest part. That's GPU time and real wall-clock time, much more than the language model reasoning.

I think that's a healthy division of labor. The LLM agents do the high-level scientific thinking: what problem to work on, which tools fit, how to combine the scores, which candidates are worth pursuing. Then they hand the heavy numerical work to specialized models built for it. You don't want a language model guessing at protein structures when AlphaFold can compute them.

And of course, the slowest step of all wasn't computational. It was the wet lab validation. Expressing the nanobodies and testing their binding against the new variants took far longer than everything the agents did put together. So the bottleneck shifts. Once the AI side gets this fast, the physical experiments become the rate-limiting step.

r001.rationale: The response says AlphaFold-Multimer predicted structures for each nanobody and that many candidate mutations were generated and evaluated, identifying this structure-prediction work as a major part of the compute.

astra-6.text: I think a lot of the computation goes into the scientists talking to each other—proposing ideas, critiquing those ideas, and then refining them. It’s not just generating a final answer. You have these different agents bringing different perspectives, and they spend time working through disagreements and checking one another’s reasoning. So much of the compute is really supporting that iterative discussion.

r001.rationale: The candidate attributes much of the computation to agents’ iterative discussion and checking, not to running AlphaFold across candidate nanobody proteins.

sol-6.1.text: My guess is that a lot of it goes into the discussion and iteration between the agents. In the Virtual Lab, the AI scientists propose ideas, critique one another’s suggestions, and then revise the plan. So you’re spending computation exploring possible approaches and checking the reasoning before settling on something to test. That back-and-forth can be valuable, but it’s also a natural place to look for ways to make the system more efficient.

r001.rationale: The response attributes computation time to discussion and iteration among agents, not to running AlphaFold across candidate nanobody proteins.
